job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Vera Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents and my grandmother in Oakley, in the house I grew up in. I get up early out of habit, help Grandma Abena with her breakfast, then sit at my desk to check job sites and send applications to civil engineering firms. After lunch I usually go to the post office or the shop for Mum, and in the evening I read the engineering news or watch a documentary about bridges. It's a quiet routine, and sometimes too quiet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you. Tell me about your degree and your internship.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied civil engineering at Ridgefield University, and my final project was the design of a small footbridge over a canal for a local walking trail. My internship was six weeks with a surveying firm, holding the staff for the senior surveyors and learning to read site drawings. I'd like a graduate role with an established firm, with a proper training scheme and a path to chartered status.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected, honestly. People get very excited about new technology and it usually ends up being useful for a few small things. I'd tell my friends that nothing's changing, so let's keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my real concern is still getting that first offer. There are plenty of firms near Oakley, but they hire graduates through two or three big schemes, and I've been rejected twice already. My savings would cover about eight months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep sending applications, but I'd ask my old surveying supervisor, Mr Dube, if he knows anybody hiring. I'd also go to the institution's local graduate evening. I wouldn't change anything about how I work, because it's working fine as it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My parents are patient, but I can see my mum watching the post for letters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've been rejected twice. What did the firms say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One sent a generic note and the other said I scored well but another candidate had more site experience. That second one stung, because I only had six weeks on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if three more months passed with nothing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably lower my sights and accept a technician job at a smaller firm, then work up. I don't love that idea, but I wouldn't sit at home forever.

I'd tell friends nothing changes, so we **keep going**.
think: My real concern is the **first offer**; I've been rejected twice already.
Firms near Oakley hire through big schemes, and savings cover about **eight months**.
do: Ask my old supervisor, Mr Dube, if he knows who's hiring.
Go to the institution's local **graduate evening**.
feel: **Uneasy**: my parents are patient, but I see Mum watching the post.
S0.quote: There are plenty of firms near Oakley, but they hire graduates through two or three big schemes
fieldNote: Her worry is the job hunt, not AI, and she reads the card **calmly**.
Rejection about site **experience** stung more than a generic reply.
Would lower her sights to a **technician** job if the wait drags on.

steps.text: Send five applications a week to civil engineering graduate schemes
Ask Mr Dube about openings at firms he knows
Attend the local engineering institution's graduate evening

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it seems like a lot of change at once and that the sensible thing is to watch how companies handle it. I'd tell friends to be careful with new tools until they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the checking and drawing jobs I'd start in are the sort of thing that goes first. Civil engineering is still hands-on, so the site side takes longer, but the entry-level desk side, the drafting and calculations, shrinks. So even fewer graduate places than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd widen my search to site engineer roles, because they involve going out and walking the ground. I'd ask about apprenticeship-style routes that mix site and design. And I'd finally try one AI tool, once a firm I'm interested in says it uses it, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I still feel I have some control, but I can see it slipping a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try an AI tool once a firm uses it. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't know which one is worth learning, and I'd rather learn what the firm uses than guess. It feels like wasted effort otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is waiting a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. Candidates who already use these tools will look more prepared than I do. I know that, and I'm still not willing to start tonight.

say: I'd say it's a lot of change at once, so companies should be **watched**.
I'd tell friends to be careful with tools until they're **proven**.
think: Drafting and calculations are where I'd start, so those **entry tasks** shrink first.
Site work lasts longer, but graduate places become **even fewer**.
do: Widen my search to **site engineer** roles.
Ask about **apprenticeship-style** routes mixing site and design.
Try one AI tool once a target firm says it uses it.
feel: **Anxious**: I still feel some control, but it's slipping.

fieldNote: Reads her own **resistance** clearly and admits it is a risk.
Moves toward site work as the **slower-moving** side of the job.
Wants to learn the tool a firm **actually** uses, not guess.

steps.text: Apply for site engineer and setting-out roles
Ask firms about site-and-design apprenticeship routes
Try the AI tool a target firm uses before the interview

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too quick for anything sensible. I'd say publicly that governments and companies must slow down and make a plan, and I'd tell my friends we need to find out what's safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm frightened. The drawing, calculating and checking I trained for would be done better by a machine within two years. Site work lasts until about 2031, but even then the firms might hire fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any civil engineering job I can find, even outside my plan, and work on site, since that's the part robots reach last. I'd keep my savings in a safe account and tell my parents what I'm doing. I'd also ask my uncle, who runs a small builder's merchant, if he has work for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can't think of what I'd do beyond that, and I don't like not having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask your uncle. How would that sit with your plan to be a chartered engineer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, but I'd do it anyway. A job on a building site that pays something is better than waiting for a graduate scheme that might shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your grandmother say about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grandma Abena says her generation survived worse and that you work with your hands. I'm not sure she's right this time, but I find it comforting.

say: Two years is **too quick** for anything sensible, so governments must slow down.
I'd tell friends we need to find out what's **safe**.
think: Drawing, calculating and checking are what I trained for, and a machine does them better within **two years**.
Site work lasts until about 2031, but firms may still hire **fewer** people.
do: Take **any civil job**, preferably on site, where robots arrive last.
Keep my savings in a **safe account**.
Ask my uncle if his builder's merchant has work.
feel: **Alarmed**, and I dislike not having a plan.
S2.quote: A job on a building site that pays something is better than waiting for a graduate scheme that might shut.
fieldNote: Drops her **chartered-status** plan for site work when time is short.
Her **grandmother's** advice comforts her though she doubts it holds.
Fear is quiet and **private**, not loud.

steps.text: Take any site-based civil engineering job offered
Keep savings in a safe account and stop non-essential spending
Ask Uncle about paid work at his builder's merchant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives time to see it coming, which suits me. I'd say that firms and universities should be honest about which roles are changing, and I'd say it politely but clearly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me five years is enough to get a first job and some experience, if I find one soon. It's the first job I worry about, because graduate schemes are the quickest to shrink. After that I might be okay for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a graduate scheme or site job within six months, then spend evenings on the chartered path. I'd start to try AI tools slowly, one at a time, once a colleague shows me how. And I'd save a third of my pay, because I'd want to be able to retrain if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a path, but I'm not sure it'll still be open when I get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said colleagues showing you. Would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I got to know someone well, yes. I'm a bit shy about asking, but a person I trust, sitting next to me, makes it so much easier than a manual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger cousin starting at university now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the degree, but get as much site experience as you can in the holidays. A person who has stood in a trench knows something a machine doesn't.

say: Five years gives time, so firms and universities should be **honest** about which roles change.
think: Five years is enough for a first job and some experience if I find one **soon**.
Graduate schemes are the **quickest to shrink**, so the first job worries me most.
do: Push for a **graduate scheme** or site job within six months.
Save a third of my pay and try AI tools when a **colleague** shows me.
feel: **Uneasy**: there's a path, but it may close before I reach it.
S3.quote: A person who has stood in a trench knows something a machine doesn't.
fieldNote: Her **caution** turns into a plan once there is time.
Learns best from a **trusted** person beside her, not a manual.
**Advises** a younger cousin to collect site hours.

steps.text: Land a graduate scheme or site job within six months
Study evenings for chartered engineer status
Ask a colleague to show me one AI tool
Save a third of every pay cheque

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels like a comfortable amount of time, though I'd tell people not to relax. I'd say governments should use it to build proper training and not leave it to chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fairly calm. By then I'd have eight or nine years of experience, maybe chartered, and I'd have learned the tools when they became normal. I'd still be on the site side, which is the last to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a normal route: first job, chartered status, a few moves up. I'd learn the AI tools at my own pace, probably around year three when they're standard. I'd keep saving and perhaps help my parents with the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little worry about the people less lucky than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tools in year three. Why not sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because by year three they'll be settled and well explained, and I won't be learning something that's out of date a month later. That's how I work, slow but sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think that approach has a cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a small one. Others will get ahead faster, but I'd rather be right than first.

steps.text: Learn standard AI tools in year three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because everything would change before anyone had made a plan. Even my careful approach wouldn't have time to work. What would help is clear information from employers and the government about which jobs are safe and which aren't, and some stability in the meantime.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd just say that not everyone wants to be the first to try something. People like me aren't against change, we just want to see it work first, and that shouldn't be treated as a flaw.

headlineQuote: People like me aren't against change, we just want to see it work first
portrait: Vera is a **23-year-old** civil engineering graduate living with her parents and grandmother, still without an offer after several months.
She is **centrist and practical** and wants a graduate scheme at an established firm, with a route to chartered status.
She **never uses AI tools** and likes change to prove itself first, which slows her down in every scenario.
Her mood is **uneasy** in the mild picture and moves to anxious and alarmed as the warning time shrinks.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because her careful, wait-and-see way would have no time to work.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **information** on which jobs are safe, plus some **stability** while things change.
